To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the sensitivity of SMC to antiproliterative agents is species dependent and the in vitro culture model does not predict the in vivo sensitivity.
the in vivo sensitivity to antiproliterative therapy is not predictable based on cell culture studies, the rat and human SMC are not appropriate for the in vitro evaluation of restenosis therapy.
the arterial explant model and SMC cultures are not suitable for predicting the in vivo efficacy of potential restenosis therapy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new drug delivery systems for local and systemic therapy of vascular restenosis.
the development of new therapeutic means to combat restenosis.
a better understanding of the in vitro/in vivo correlation and with the development of an in vitro model for the screening of antirestenotic drug candidates.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
in vitro SMC cultures are of limited value for the prediction of the therapeutic efficacy of drugs in restenosis therapy.
the arterial explant model and SMC cultures are of limited use in predicting the in vivo effects of potential antiproliferating drugs in restenosis therapy.
in vitro studies are not suitable for the screening of potential restenosis drugs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the in vitro SMC culture model is not suitable for screening antiproliferation drugs for restenosis, but it may provide a useful tool to evaluate the efficacy of controlled release drug delivery systems.
the SMC cultures of rabbit and porcine are not suitable for prescreening antiproliferating drugs for restenosis.
the arterial explant model and SMC cultures are not appropriate for screening antirestenosis drugs.
The main takeaway from our work is that

cell cultures of rat or rabbit SMC are not suitable for the prescreening of drugs for antirestenotic therapy, and that the explant out-growth model is not suitable for the prediction of drug efficacy in the rat.

the species sensitivity to antiprolifterative drugs and drug delivery systems is different from the species susceptibility to restenosis, which is the main cause of failure of in vitro prescreening studies.
in vitro cell culture systems should be validated with in vivo models prior to use in the screening of new drug candidates.
